newsitem.title: UK: Yen to keep pressure on dollar, eyes on trade data.
newsitem.headline: Yen to keep pressure on dollar, eyes on trade data.

text.p: The yen looks set to keep the upper hand against the dollar as this week's economic data underline a burgeoning trade gap which analysts fear could create friction between the United States and Japan at the forthcoming G7 summit.
But economists say major price moves are unlikely as the forex market has already felt the brunt of bilateral friction over Japan's current account surplus.
The dollar, which tumbled to a six-month low against the yen last week, slipped in early Europe on Tuesday to 113.22/32 yen from late Monday's 113.45/55.
But it was sturdy against the mark after EU leaders on Monday reached agreement on a pact to ensure budgetary rigour under monetary union.
"The dollar is gaining against European currencies, but we have seen a shift in dollar/yen, not just in sentiment but in fundamentals," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ.
The yen has been rising against the U.S. unit since early May amid mounting concern that increased trade friction with the United States was on the horizon.
"We're going to have a fairly well-bid yen ahead of the G7 summit, given the concerns that have been expressed about Japan's trade surplus," said Edmonds.
"We've got further yen strength to come, but I don't think we'll see a major move -- even after the summit. The yen's likely to consolidate around current levels first."

Influential Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara sparked a leap in the dollar last week when he said Japan's trade surplus, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, was no cause for concern.

After declining last year, when the weak yen depressed the value of exports, the balance of payments surplus has since rocketed in Japan, a country which has minimal restrictions on exports but numerous quotas on imports.
The rise prompted U.S. officials to warn that a widening bilateral trade imbalance was unacceptable.
Officials, including an IMF source, have dismissed speculation they will focus on the trade situation when the Group of Seven meets in Denver, Colorado on June 20-22.
A show of unity between the U.S. and Japan should allow a period of relative stability in dollar/yen, said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Economists polled by Reuters predict Japan's trade surplus for May, to be revealed at 2350 GMT on Tuesday, will widen to 548.5 billion yen from 229 billion in April. That compares to an expected U.S. trade deficit, due Thursday, of $10 billion for April versus $8.5 billion previously.

Lehman Brothers foreign exchange economist Francis Breedon said Japan's current account would eventually correct itself according to the 'J-curve' principle, as trade volumes responded to higher consumption of imports cheapened by the exchange rate.
"It'll look terrifying for a couple of months," said Breedon, "but it'll come down later in the year."
He said the Bank of Japan's quarterly Tankan survey of corporations -- due out next Tuesday -- would be critical in gauging the state of the Japanese economy.
Meanwhile, Breedon said, the dollar's support in Europe should not be taken for granted.

EU leaders meeting on Monday reached accord on a pact designed to ensure a stable euro after its 1999 launch. The pact, thrown into question when France last week requested extra time to study it, included a resolution on jobs and growth.
However, analysts said the important question remained whether monetary union would encompass weaker European economies such as Italy and Spain.
The market's preoccupation with the single currency has enabled the dollar to shrug off fading market expectations of fresh U.S. Federal Reserve tightening, analysts said.
After a surprise fall in U.S. May PPI on Friday, CPI data due on Tuesday are expected to show inflationary pressure remaining subdued.
